Table 2. Bill of materials and measured system characteristics.

Figure 1. System design and counting workflow. (a) Imaging rig: downward-facing camera on an adjustable crossbar, transparent tray on a backlit LED panel, Raspberry Pi with accelerator and touchscreen, all within an open aluminium frame. (b) Counting workflow from tray placement through on-device inference to displayed count and accumulated batch total. (c) Evaluation design linking first-harvest training and internal leave-one-load-out testing, accelerator compilation with paired framework and compiled evaluation, and external validation of frozen artifacts on a second harvest. The rig illustration is schematic; the tray is 15 × 15 cm, and the lens-to-panel distance is 20 cm.
Table 3. Dataset populations and their roles.

Figure 2. Accepted body-centre annotations at sparse, intermediate and crowded count levels (71, 501 and 1,577 accepted points). Blue squares locate equal 260 × 260-pixel crops; magenta circles mark retained body-centre coordinates. Each point denotes one distinguishable individual. The crowded example illustrates the overlap regime in which instance separation becomes unreliable and density regression is required.

Figure 3. Implemented counting architectures. Each maps a 1280 × 1280 RGB image to a 160 × 160 density map whose spatial sum gives the count. IR denotes inverted residual; S denotes input-relative stride. MobileCount uses additive skip fusion; YOLO26n-density uses the concatenation-based neck of its source detector, terminating at the P3 tensor. Supervision recipes alter training only and add no inference-time layers.

Figure 4. Internal evaluation on the first harvest. (a) Error per held-out load for all eleven configurations, with within-range and out-of-range folds distinguished; note the change of scale between panels. (b) Systematic-offset index S against MAE for every configuration–fold combination; points approaching S = 1 identify loads in which every image erred in the same direction. (c) Held-out load reference-count distributions against the training range for each fold, showing which loads fall outside it. [Panel (c) requires the per-fold count ranges noted in Section 6.1]

Figure 5. Agreement between model and reference counts for the two leading configurations on within-range folds, plotted as the difference against the mean of the two measures. Solid line, mean difference; dashed lines, 95% limits of agreement; shaded band, the 22.60-animal disagreement between repeat annotations. Each point is one held-out image (n = 1,280 per panel).

Figure 6. Proportion of held-out within-range images counted within ±k% of the reference count, as a function of tolerance k. (a) All eleven configurations; thick lines with markers denote the best configuration within each architecture, thin lines the remaining eight. (b) The same data read at a ±2% operating point, ordered by value. n = 1,280 per configuration.

Figure 7. Dependence of counting error on density. (a) Proportional-bias slope for each configuration with 95% confidence intervals, ordered by slope; the shaded band marks the ±1% region treated as immaterial. Marker shape and colour denote architecture. (b) The mechanism on common axes: YOLO26n-density under Gaussian supervision drifts at +0.0227 animals per animal of true count, while MobileCount under reference optimal transport with the Bayesian loss is flat at +0.0021. Points are individual held-out images; lines are ordinary least-squares fits.
Table 8. Agreement with the reference annotation on within-range folds, with tolerance and proportional-bias summaries. n = 1,280 held-out images per configuration.

Figure 8. External validation on the second harvest. (a) Compiled accuracy per configuration with the three individual checkpoint scores retained, illustrating the difference in checkpoint spread between the reference model and the compact configurations; the dashed line marks the 22.60-animal repeatability of the annotation reference. (b) Rank concordance between evaluation stages, showing that internal ranking does not predict external ranking. (c) Accuracy against inference-call latency, identifying the operating points available to a deployment.

Figure 9. Per-configuration equivalence between the quantized framework model and the compiled artifact on the second harvest, ordered by verdict. Thick bars, 90% confidence interval on the mean difference; thin whiskers, 95% limits of agreement; shaded band, the ±20.4-animal equivalence margin (2% of the mean second-harvest count). Equivalence requires both the confidence interval and the limits of agreement to fall inside the margin. n = 3,633 paired images per configuration.
Table 9. Two one-sided tests of equivalence between framework and compiled inference, second harvest.

Figure 10. Within-range agreement against on-device latency for all eleven configurations. The vertical axis is the agreement half-width of Table 8; the horizontal axis is mean latency per inference call, on a broken scale because ten configurations fall within 45.6–49.1 ms and one at 215.2 ms. Marker area is proportional to parameter count; colour and shape denote architecture; the dashed line marks the Pareto frontier. Latency covers the inference call only and excludes capture, decoding, host preprocessing and map summation, so the throughput values are not end-to-end tray rates. The ordering shown here is reversed by the external validation of Section 7.6.

Table 10. Deployment and execution characteristics of reported counting systems. Accuracy is deliberately omitted: the studies address different organisms at different densities under different annotation conventions and their error figures are not commensurable (Section 2.5).
